extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and advanced law students working on patent litigation and prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: A compilation of doctrinal standards and procedural criteria governing patent applications, Office practice, and patent litigation (actions at law and in equity), including evidence rules, pleadings, remedies, damages, and appellate practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting in equity — plaintiff must give sufficient data
rubrics_metrics.description: On an accounting, the plaintiff must give sufficient data; account must be certain; admissibility of evidence in accounting governed by specified rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes rules on burden of proof, objections/exceptions, presumed inability of defendant to overcome plaintiff's proof unless he does so, that neither court nor master should suggest what is needed, admissions in answer as evidence, inspection of defendant's books, and treatment of opinions and amounts paid by defendant or others. License-fees and settlement amounts treated specially (see related items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in accounting and damages
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of proof in accounting proceedings and on damages rests largely on the plaintiff, with specific presumptions and standards described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presumptions favor plaintiff's evidence in many respects; plaintiff must show how much of defendant's gains are due to the patented invention; burden as to computation and separation of items; plaintiff's evidence favored and liberally construed in equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility of evidence without prior notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain evidence (prior patents, publications, prior use, abandonment, etc.) is not admissible at trial without timely notice to the opposing party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Various categories (prior patent, prior publication, prior use, abandonment to the public) require specific notice; evidence offered without such notice may be considered only for limited purposes (e.g., state of the art) or be excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection of defendant's books and accounting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may inspect defendant's books; such documentary evidence is central to computing profits and damages in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules cover what documentary evidence is admissible, how receipts and savings are treated, and which items of cost are allowable; items not supported by evidence may be struck out.

rubrics_metrics.name: License fees as measure of damages — when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: License fees may be the proper measure of damages where plaintiff grants licenses broadly (preserves a monopoly by licensing) or where defendant does exactly the licensed act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between when license fee is measure (e.g., plaintiff grants licenses to all comers) and when it is not (defendant's use differs in duration or extent); rules on evidence establishing license fee and implied acceptance by defendant are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amounts paid in settlement or as royalties by others not always admissible
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts paid by third parties in settlement or as royalties are generally not admissible as measure of damages without proper context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such amounts may be treated with caution; see specific notes on when they may or may not be persuasive or admissible as evidence of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft report of master inadmissible after filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A master's draft report is inadmissible after it has been filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers filed with master pending an accounting and draft reports have specific evidentiary constraints; objections to master's reports and exceptions proceed under enumerated procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final report of master — exceptions and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Final reports of masters are subject to exceptions and have a stated procedure for court review; items not supported by evidence may be struck out or recommitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may set aside or correct awards for erroneous damages or profits, recommit for amendment or further hearing (e.g., for excessive damages); masters' findings on matters of fact generally not reviewed except as specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of profits and damages in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits and damages must be pecuniary, computed (not conjectured), and determined according to the form of infringement and the nature of the invention; cannot include remote or contingent benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mode of computation depends on form of infringement (sales, use, commissions, repairs); measured by difference between cost and yield when appropriate; must separate profits attributable to improvements vs original invention; items of cost allowable and burden on plaintiff to show computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits not computable cannot be awarded
rubrics_metrics.description: If profits are not capable of computation, courts cannot award them as profits in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When actual computation is impossible, remedies are constrained; alternative remedies may be sought but profits require ascertainable computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest on profits and damages — when recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Interest on awarded profits or damages is recoverable only in certain circumstances as stipulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See referenced rules specifying when interest may be added to accounts or damages (e.g., interest provisions in equity accounting and damages at law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel fees generally not recoverable in equity accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel fees are not ordinarily recoverable as part of an accounting or as damages in equity actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are narrow exceptions; but generally costs and counsel fees follow statutory and equitable rules limiting recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions — scope, interlocutory/final, and rehearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunction practice rules cover interlocutory decrees, when final decrees issue, rehearings (when allowed), and when injunctions will or will not be granted (e.g., laches, adequacy of legal remedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes that courts will not grant injunctions against officers of solvent corporations unless they also infringe, will not order delivery-up for destruction, may suspend pending other actions, and rehearing rules (new evidence, supplemental bills, new defenses). Rules of practice bind circuit courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decrees — when patent void on its face mandates dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may declare a patent void on its face and deny equitable relief when the patent is invalid on its face or when plaintiff has no legal or equitable interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patent is void on its face, equivalents include dismissal for lack of interest; rules also discuss when equitable relief not appropriate due to laches or passage of time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action at law — who may be plaintiff (party interested)
rubrics_metrics.description: An action at law for infringement must be brought by a 'party interested' — typically the patentee, an assignee, or grantee; licensees and equitable owners have limited standing unless nominal legal owner is joined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local law may affect who may sue; assignors, assignees in trust, co-owners, executors, and grantees of exclusive rights have specific rules; licensees generally not proper plaintiffs absent special circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and venue in actions at law
rubrics_metrics.description: Venue lies in any district where the defendant can be served; rules vary when circuits include several districts and for joint-infringers or foreign corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes discussion of service on domestic and foreign corporations and the effect of various statutes (e.g., acts referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration/pleading contents — must tender issues on patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The declaration (pleading) must contain averments sufficient to tender an issue on every point essential to patentability, description of the invention, title, and statement of infringement and damages as required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal requisites and defects; a declaration on the case is usually sufficient; averments must be as broad as evidence required; variances between pleading and patent are treated carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings and special pleas — notice and requisites for defences
rubrics_metrics.description: Special pleas (e.g., prior use, prior patent, publication, abandonment) have particular requisites and often require notice; statute of limitations must be specially pleaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requisites spelled out for pleas of prior use, prior patent/publication, abandonment to the public, and fraudulent specification; some pleas must state particulars (e.g., names of users) and may be struck if defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent presumed valid — weight and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is presumed valid; the patent shows regularity of grant, sufficiency of specification, and legal title in the patentee, with weight increased by re-issue or extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant bears burden to prove invalidity of a re-issue (e.g., by offering original and showing discrepancy); presumptions affect admissibility and proof obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence rules in patent trials — documentary and expert evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules govern admissibility and weight of documentary records, former judgments, witnesses, competency, expert testimony, and order of production; expert evidence has distinct classes, weight, and admissibility conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert evidence admissible under specific criteria, may be excluded by estoppel, and has rules on weight and competency. Documentary evidence (e.g., file wrapper, prior application) has particular limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of the art evidence — purpose and admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of the state of the art is admissible (sometimes without notice) to show what was known, but admitted without notice is typically considered only for that limited purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior publication used to show date and content of the state of art; such evidence may be admissible without notice for limited purposes but not to raise new defenses absent notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages at law — rules differ from equity and proof requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Recovery of damages at law differs from equitable recovery; rules of evidence and measures differ depending on how plaintiff enjoyed monopoly (licenses vs making/selling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actual damages must be clearly proved; recoverable only to the date of the writ (in many cases); indirect evidence allowed in certain contexts; remote and contingent items ordinarily inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of damages when plaintiff sells product vs grants licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: When plaintiff sells product, damages arise from price reduction or loss of sales; when plaintiff grants licenses, license fee may be the measure of damages if defendant performs the exact licensed act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules of evidence differ: direct and indirect evidence distinctions; demonstration of monopoly enjoyment affects admissibility and measure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal damages — when awarded and rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominal damages are awarded in limited circumstances where actual loss cannot be shown; courts have specific rules about when nominal damages are proper and when they should be set aside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes that nominal damages have particular rules and may be awarded where proof of substantial damages fails but liability is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counsel fees and costs at law generally not recoverable
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel fees and expenses of suit are generally not recoverable as damages at law except under specific statutes or narrow equitable exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment characterized as creating future license in some contexts; courts constrain inclusion of counsel fees as part of damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial questions — jury vs court and allocation of issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules on what issues are for court and what are for jury; trials by court without jury have specific procedures; charges to jury, requests, and exceptions governed by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matters like patent invalidity on its face may require directed verdicts for defendant; continuance rules, nonsuit equivalents, new trials, and grounds for writ of error are addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application for patent — required parts and form
rubrics_metrics.description: An application must contain petition, oath, specification, and sometimes drawings and a model; must be in English; all parts must be filed within specified time and be complete for filing to be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal requisites must be met; application is evidence of date and can be presumed regular; parts filed separately require connecting letter; filing date rules, secrecy, and continuity defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification and claim — must cover patentable matter shown
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim covers only the matter claimed, but the specification covers all patentable matter shown in the specification, drawings, or model; claims must not contradict disclaimers and must be supported by description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Description and claims treated separately though construed together; disclaimers must explain claim and not contradict it; ambiguity in description or claims can be fatal; excessive or ambiguous claims scrutinized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath in application — truthfulness and effects of falsehood
rubrics_metrics.description: The application oath must be true as to each part of the specification; material and willful falsehood avoids the patent, though some falsehoods may not avoid it depending on circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office generally cannot inquire into the truth of the oath after grant; false oath avoidance requires proof of materiality and willfulness; renewals of oath required on amendments that introduce new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing date, continuity, and relation between successive applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing date is the commencement of proceedings; continuity, divisionals, and successive applications have precise rules determining which applications get the earlier date and how continuity is tested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous applications may take original filing date if proper; divisionals require specific procedure and cross-disclaimers; decision of Commissioner on filing is conclusive in many respects; tests of continuity provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisionals and misjoinder — examiner's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may object for misjoinder and order division of applications when multiple inventions are claimed; divisionals require new oath and cross-disclaimers as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure for making divisions, when ordered, and how parts filed separately must be connected; examiner must address misjoinder and explain mode of avoiding form objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination and rejection — examiner must cite references and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: On rejection, the examiner must state the references relied upon and give reasons in the notice; examination on merit is governed by court rules and prior decisions but is not bound by former examiners' conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner decides patentability from any available data, must require form sufficiency before merit determinations, and may remand or involve examiners-in-chief and Commissioner in appeal procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection for impracticability and procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner should reject an application if the invention is evidently impracticable; procedure for notice, remand, and appeals specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and references discussed; rejected applicants have appeal rights within reasonable time and may seek equity if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal in Patent Office — scope and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals in the Patent Office in uncontested cases proceed by distinct administrative procedures resembling equity appeals; matters of form are decided by Commissioner, matters of substance by examiners-in-chief, with further avenues to Commissioner and courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must act twice before Commissioner review in some cases; appeals are not writs of error; remands, recommendations, and procedures in interferences and contested matters outlined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses to infringement — novelty, utility, prior use, public use, abandonment, fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses include lack of inventive act, want of novelty, prior patent/publication/use, abandonment to the public, lack of utility, fraudulent specification, ambiguity, excessive or ambiguous claims, surrender or repeal of patent, and denial of plaintiff's title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each defense has particular requisites of pleading and proof; many require notice in pleadings; courts treat each defense with established evidentiary rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of prior use/publication — particular rules and notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of prior use or publication has strict admissibility rules, often requiring notice; discrepancies and variances reduce admissibility; such evidence may serve to show dates and knowledge of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior use must meet requisites; prior publication not admissible without notice in many instances; publications not named in notice may not be admitted to show certain facts.
